title: LDSCI6253 Week 2 · Visual Communication (transform, then figure)

slides.name: 1 · Visual Communication

params.text: LDSCI6253 WEEK 2 · VISUAL COMMUNICATION (TRANSFORM, THEN FIGURE)

slides.notes:
0–5 min. Welcome back. Week 1 introduced why we visualise and the What–Why–How framework. Today connects data types to visual choices. Ask: what made one chart from last week memorable? Plan: foundations 10 min, integrity 25 min, data and channels 25 min, colour 15 min, critique and questions 15 min. Allow a short pause around the data-abstraction divider. The cover is the Northeastern title layout, so the date is the layout’s own stamp and the subtitle does not repeat it.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 2 · What you will practise

params.text:
Distinguish categorical, ordinal and quantitative attributes.
Match a visual channel to a comparison task.
Explain how a chart can distort its data.
Critique a design using perceptual evidence.

slides.notes:
Read these as promises you intend to keep. The fourth is the one that changes how they argue in the lab: 'I don't like it' becomes 'that channel cannot carry that data'.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 7 · Data, encoding and perception

params.text:
Data: the values and relationships to communicate.
Encoding: the marks and channels that represent them.
Perception: how a viewer interprets those marks.

slides.notes:
Visual communication uses visual elements to convey information. In this lesson the aim is understanding, insight and decisions. Ask students for a failure at each stage. Inaccurate data, an unsuitable channel and an unclear legend can each undermine a chart.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 8 · What a good chart has to do

params.text: What a good chart has to do
It conveys the information you intended, accurately.
It costs the reader as little effort as possible to understand.
It looks considered, and belongs where it is published.

slides.notes:
The three primary goals from the supplied Week 2 deck. Say that they are ranked: an efficient, handsome chart of the wrong quantity is still a failure. Efficiency is the one students under-weight, because they read their own chart fluently — they already know what it says.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 9 · The design brief

params.text:
What should the audience understand?
Who will read the chart?
What decision or question will it support?
Will they see a slide, report or interactive display?

slides.notes:
The third is the one that changes designs. 'What decision gets made from this' turns a chart of everything into a chart of the thing that matters. Ask the room for their AE1 answer to it.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 12 · Three trade-offs you cannot avoid

params.text: Cut until the message is clear; the next cut takes the evidence with it.
A new idiom buys attention and spends comprehension.
When the two disagree, the reader’s answer decides it.

slides.notes:
Trade-offs, not rules: each one is a dial that the design brief sets, which is why the brief comes first. Ask the room which dial their own coursework chart has set wrongly, and what it was bought with.

slides.name: 14 · Section · Graphical integrity

params.text: Tufte's question: does the picture say what the numbers say?

slides.notes:
The spine of the lecture. Everything from here to the rules of thumb is one argument — the graphic is a measurement, and a measurement can be wrong.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 15 · Tufte’s six principles of graphical integrity

params.text: Tufte’s six principles of graphical integrity
Measured size on the page stays proportional to the quantity.
Label thoroughly; write the explanation on the graphic itself.
Show data variation, not design variation.
For money over time, deflated units beat nominal ones.
Never use more dimensions than the data has.
Do not quote data out of context.

slides.notes:
Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. The rows are shortened to fit; his wording is: (1) the representation of numbers, as physically measured on the surface of the graphic itself, should be directly proportional to the numerical quantities represented; (2) clear, detailed and thorough labelling should be used to defeat graphical distortion and ambiguity — write out explanations of the data on the graphic itself, label important events in the data; (3) show data variation, not design variation; (4) in time-series displays of money, deflated and standardised units of monetary measurement are nearly always better than nominal units; (5) the number of information-carrying (variable) dimensions depicted should not exceed the number of dimensions in the data; (6) graphics must not quote data out of context.

The supplied Week 2 deck announces six and prints five, because the last two are run together in one paragraph; they are separated here. Principles 1 and 5 are the ones the lie factor and the 3D examples test later in this section. Principle 4 is the one nobody applies until they plot a decade of prices.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials (01_Lecture_IPDV_2_2, slide 10).

slides.name: 17 · Your redesign proposal

params.text:
Let's say that these represent the polling from a local election with five candidates, at three different points A, B and C during the campaign:
In the first poll, is candidate 5 doing better than candidate 3?
Who did better between time A and time B, candidate 2 or candidate 4?
Who has the most momentum in the race?

slides.notes:
Shown after the transformation. This is the figure the animated states replace — use it to name the published convention once students have made and tested their own prediction.
5 min including discussion. Deliberately revisit the opening exercise to assess transfer. A bar chart is reasonable for candidate comparison; a line chart can help track change over A, B and C. Require a stated task, labels and a justification. Do not invent sampling uncertainty absent from the source. Ask what metadata would be needed to assess whether a change is meaningful.

slides.name: 18 · Your redesign proposal

params.text: Click to go through each numbered detail in order.
1  Three polls, the same five candidates

A, B and C are the same election at three moments. Candidates 1 to 5 keep their colour and their left-to-right position in every panel, so the eye can follow one candidate across time. Poll A: 17, 18, 20, 22, 23. Poll B: 20, 20, 19, 21, 20. Poll C: 23, 22, 20, 18, 17.
2  One scale, shared by all three

Every panel runs 0 to 25 from the same zero baseline. That is what the pie charts could not give you: length here is proportional to the count, and lengths in different panels mean the same thing. Tufte’s first principle, doing its work.
3  Poll A — is candidate 5 ahead of candidate 3?

Yes. Candidate 5 is on 23, candidate 3 on 20 — a three-point lead you can see as a difference in bar length. In the pie you were comparing two angles that did not share an edge, which is why nobody could answer it with confidence.
4  A to B — candidate 2 or candidate 4?

Candidate 2 did better. They go 18 to 20, a two-point gain, while candidate 4 goes 22 to 21 and slips by one. Reading the same slot in two panels makes this a comparison of position rather than an act of memory.
5  Poll C — who has the momentum?

Candidate 1. Across the three polls they go 17, 20, 23 — six points gained — while candidate 5 runs 23, 20, 17 the other way. Poll C is the mirror image of Poll A, and the reversal is visible as a shape rather than recalled from numbers.
Every detail, back in its place.

slides.name: 20 · Graphical integrity

params.text: The values stay at 100 and 110. How much bigger does the second bar look?

params.data:
Group	Value
A	100
B	110
params.source: Synthetic teaching examples, not observed research data.
params.prompt: The values stay at 100 and 110. How much bigger does the second bar look?

slides.notes:
Predict first, then advance one state at a time. Replay change retraces the previous transformation. Ask students to name the changing visual channel and the data that stays fixed.
Zero baseline: 110 is 10% greater than 100. Bar lengths preserve that comparison.
Baseline at 90: DELIBERATE DISTORTION: visible lengths are 10 and 20. A 10% data increase appears as a 100% length increase. Lie factor = 10.
Baseline at 95: DELIBERATE DISTORTION: visible lengths are 5 and 15. The graphic shows a 200% increase. Lie factor = 20.
Restore context: A bar encodes length. Restoring zero restores the relationship between length and quantity.

slides.name: 21 · The lie factor

params.text: Relative change in the graphic ÷ relative change in the data

slides.notes:
Use relative changes with the same reference value. Example: data rises from 100 to 110, a 10% increase. A graphic rising from 10 mm to 30 mm shows a 200% increase. Lie factor = 200/10 = 20. A value near 1 preserves the relative effect. The supplied historical fuel-economy example uses 783/53 ≈ 14.8. A zero baseline matters for bar length. A line chart need not start at zero, but its scale and context must remain clear.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 22 · The lie factor, measured

params.text: The New York Times fuel-economy graphic, and the arithmetic on it

Effect in the graphic: 783.

Effect in the data: 53.

Lie factor = 14.8. Honest is 1.0.

slides.notes:
The worked example behind the definition on the slide before. The graphic exaggerates the effect by 783 to 53 — a lie factor of 14.8, where 1.0 is honest. Walk the two numbers out loud: the size of the effect shown, over the size of the effect in the data.
Source: figure from the supplied Week 2 lecture deck (01_Lecture_IPDV_2_2).

slides.name: 23 · Facing the Nation

params.text: Chernoff faces, and design variation standing in for data variation

Several attributes, one mark.

The eye reads faces well, and reads their measurements badly.

slides.notes:
The counter-example for "show data variation, not design variation". Each face encodes several variables at once in features we are evolved to read — which is the appeal — but small changes in feature shape are not read proportionally, so the encoding flatters some differences and hides others. A memorable figure to argue with rather than to copy.
Source: figure from the supplied Week 2 lecture deck (01_Lecture_IPDV_2_2).

slides.name: 28 · Common sources of distortion

params.text: Can the same observations appear to tell different stories?

params.source: Synthetic teaching examples, not observed research data.
params.prompt: Can the same observations appear to tell different stories?

slides.notes:
Predict first, then advance one state at a time. Replay change retraces the previous transformation. Ask students to name the changing visual channel and the data that stays fixed.
Complete series: The whole six-period series shows fluctuations and an overall increase.
Compressed width: The values and scale are unchanged. A narrow plot makes the slopes look steeper.
Selected ending: DELIBERATELY SELECTED RANGE: periods 4–6 suggest decline. The earlier observations provide different context.

slides.name: 29 · Occlusion and distortion

params.text: Two ways a three-dimensional chart hides its own data

Occlusion — the near series hides the far ones.

Distortion — perspective changes apparent size.

slides.notes:
Occlusion: the front series hides the ones behind it, so values simply cannot be read. Distortion: perspective makes the near side of a ring larger than the far side, so equal quantities look unequal. Neither is a styling preference — both remove information the chart claims to show.
Source: figure from the supplied Week 2 lecture deck (01_Lecture_IPDV_2_2).

slides.name: 31 · Cumulative and quarterly sales
slides.notes:
Use the before/after reveal. The supplied Apple graphic shows cumulative iPhone sales. The Quartz comparison adds quarterly sales. Ask: can total sales rise while quarterly sales fall? Yes: positive sales add to the total even when the quarterly rate falls. Cumulative totals can plateau, so avoid saying they always rise. These are historical source images, not current sales figures.
Source: adapted from the supplied Week 2 lecture materials.

slides.name: 32 · Design Principles and Rules of Thumb

params.text: Design Principles and Rules of Thumb

Keep marks that explain the data.
Remove decoration that competes with the comparison.
Retain useful labels, reference lines and context.

slides.notes:
Shown after the transformation. This is the figure the animated states replace — use it to name the published convention once students have made and tested their own prediction.
Tufte’s data-ink principle is a design heuristic. A bare chart is not automatically better. Ask which elements in the source examples help interpretation and which obstruct it. Distinguish memorability from numerical accuracy.

slides.name: 34 · Miller’s law

params.text: How much the room can hold while it reads your chart

Sensing: many chunks arrive at once.

Remembering: roughly seven, plus or minus two.

slides.notes:
The reason decluttering is not a matter of taste. Working memory holds only a handful of chunks, so every decorative element competes with the comparison you are asking for. Use it to justify the previous slide rather than asserting "less is more".

slides.name: 37 · Four dataset structures

params.text: What is an item, a link, a field or a spatial boundary?

params.data:
Station	Hires
A	20
B	35
C	60
D	80
params.source: Synthetic teaching examples, not observed research data.
params.prompt: What is an item, a link, a field or a spatial boundary?

slides.notes:
Predict first, then advance one state at a time. Replay change retraces the previous transformation. Ask students to name the changing visual channel and the data that stays fixed.
Table: Each row is an item. Station is an identifier and hires is an attribute.
Network: Nodes represent stations; lines represent hypothetical connections. Links need their own data.
Field: A synthetic temperature field sampled across space. Each location has a value, rather than a named station.

slides.name: 46 · Attribute types

params.text: Do the values have order, meaningful differences, or meaningful ratios?

slides.notes:
Predict first, then advance one state at a time. Replay change retraces the previous transformation. Ask students to name the changing visual channel and the data that stays fixed.
Nominal: Numbers can be names. Station 12 is not four times Station 3.

slides.name: 47 · Check · Attribute types · 1

params.text: T-shirt sizes; S, M, L, XL. What kind of attribute is that?
Categorical — the labels are just names
Ordinal — ordered, but the gaps are not measurable
Quantitative interval — ordered with equal gaps, no true zero
Quantitative ratio — ordered with equal gaps and a true zero

slides.notes:

params.text: Which encoding makes close quantities easiest to compare?

params.source: Synthetic teaching examples, not observed research data.
params.prompt: Which encoding makes close quantities easiest to compare?

slides.notes:
Predict first, then advance one state at a time. Replay change retraces the previous transformation. Ask students to name the changing visual channel and the data that stays fixed.
Position: Points share a vertical scale. Compare their positions.
Area: Circle AREA represents value, so radius scales with the square root. Close comparisons become harder.
Hue only: Hue identifies categories but has no inherent numerical order. Labels are doing the quantitative work here.
Shape: Different symbols identify categories. Their shapes do not encode the numeric values.
Length: Bars encode the same quantities by length from a shared zero baseline.

params.text: You are mapping profit and loss by region, where zero matters. Which colour scheme?
